title: QuantaPay x Redwood — POC weekly check-in (bench results + case study metrics wording)
summary: Weekly POC check-in. QuantaPay shared early benchmark results from traffic replay against Redwood Dedicated: strong p50 improvements and stable throughput, but a p95 latency regression appeared in one window (likely batch/queueing + a model build change). Team aligned on next debugging steps and agreed on how to phrase performance/cost outcomes for a public case study (scoped claims, explicit workload parameters, and validation window). Security reiterated that any public write-up must avoid exact request volumes, region details, and internal model names.
topics: POC benchmark status (traffic replay, acceptance thresholds)
p95 latency regression observed in a specific window
Rate limits / retry behavior and occasional 429s
Cost-per-request / cost per 1K tokens framing for a case study
What can/can’t be published publicly (security + procurement constraints)
Next week plan: rerun with fixed build, narrower batching limits, capture traces
action_items: Markus Klein (Redwood) — Pull Console traces for 2025-06-03 14:00–16:00 PT window and correlate queue time vs token time; share readout with QuantaPay by 2025-06-07
Ravi Iyer (QuantaPay) — Confirm exact replay parameters (prompt/output length distribution, concurrency ramp, retries) and send the run config + Grafana screenshots by 2025-06-06
Sana Farid (Redwood) — Propose “publishable metrics” table w/ wording options (p50/p95, cost/query) including caveats and measurement window; send draft to Soojin + Elena by 2025-06-10
Priyom Das (Redwood) — Schedule a 45-min technical deep dive early next week incl. Redwood runtime engineer if needed; propose times by EOD 2025-06-05
Dinesh Patel (QuantaPay) — Provide list of prohibited disclosure items for public case study (regions, volumes, internal system names) by 2025-06-11
next_steps: Rerun benchmark on the same model version/build used in the “good” window and compare p95; keep all other variables constant
Temporarily cap batching to reduce tail latency and measure throughput impact (Dedicated pool)
Align on a single published claim: “X% lower p95 latency at Y throughput in production-like replay,” with explicit query shape ranges (no exact customer volumes)
If p95 regression persists, Redwood to open/attach support ticket and provide an RCA-style note suitable for internal only (not for public case study)
transcript:
Fireflies.ai Transcript

Meeting: QuantaPay x Redwood — POC weekly check-in (bench results + case study metrics wording)
Date: Jun 5, 2025 10:00 AM PT
Duration: 36 min

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Priyom Das (AE), Markus Klein (SE), Sana Farid (Metrics/Measurement), Soojin Lee (Product Marketing)
QuantaPay: Elena Park (Head of ML Platform), Ravi Iyer (Staff Eng), Maya Chen (PM), Dinesh Patel (Security)

---

[00:00] Priyom Das: Cool, I think we’re all here. Elena, Ravi, Maya, Dinesh — thanks. This is the weekly POC check-in. Goal today: go over the replay results you ran, talk through the tail latency blip we saw, and then Soojin joined because you asked about “how do we say this” for the case study if we hit the targets.

[00:22] Elena Park: Yep, thanks. We’re… cautiously happy? p50 looks great. p95 we have a question mark.

[00:31] Markus Klein: That’s usually the right mood for week two. (laughs) Ravi, do you want to share what you’re seeing?

[00:40] Ravi Iyer: Sure. So we ran the traffic replay job Tuesday and again yesterday. Tuesday’s run, the p50 was down a lot versus our vLLM baseline. Yesterday, between like… two and four PM Pacific, p95 jumped. We didn’t change the replay harness, to our knowledge.

[01:01] Markus Klein: When you say “jumped,” is it like queue time or token time, or do we know?

[01:08] Ravi Iyer: We don’t know yet. We’re just looking at the client side timers plus the dashboard you gave us.

[01:15] Sana Farid: And you have both “time to first token” and “total latency,” right?

[01:18] Ravi Iyer: Yeah. TTFT stayed mostly okay, but total p95 got worse.

[01:24] Maya Chen: And from product perspective, the total is what users feel because our UX waits for the final structured output.

[01:31] Priyom Das: Got it. So Tuesday was good, Wednesday had a bad window.

[01:37] Elena Park: Correct. And for us the acceptance is p95 under our threshold during peak-like conditions. We don’t need you to be magic at p99 right now, but p95 has to behave.

[01:50] Markus Klein: Makes sense. Let me ask a few “annoying” questions. Was the model pinned to the same version? And same quant profile?

[02:00] Ravi Iyer: We pinned the model ID you gave. But I saw in the Console it says “build” something something. Could have changed?

[02:07] Markus Klein: Yeah, okay. That’s important. There was a hotfix build for the kernel selection last week. It shouldn’t worsen tail, but let’s not assume.

[02:17] Sana Farid: Also the shape distribution matters. If your replay had a longer tail of outputs in that window, that would show up in total latency.

[02:26] Ravi Iyer: We didn’t change the sample set. But the replay does have a concurrency ramp. So maybe we crossed a queueing knee.

[02:33] Markus Klein: That’s my first hypothesis: batcher and queue time. Especially if we’re trying to push throughput and you cross the “continuous batching” sweet spot.

[02:42] Elena Park: Is that something we can tune on Dedicated, or is it fixed?

[02:46] Markus Klein: On Dedicated we can tune max batch tokens, max waiting time, and a couple of other constraints. Right now we set it pretty aggressive to hit your throughput goal.

[02:56] Priyom Das: And that’s part of why Dedicated is nice here — we’re not sharing with random neighbors.

[03:02] Dinesh Patel: Just to confirm, “Dedicated” means isolated GPU pool, yes? No data mixing.

[03:07] Priyom Das: Correct. Isolated pool. Separate tenant boundary. We can send the standard language again, but yes.

[03:12] Dinesh Patel: Okay.

[03:14] Markus Klein: Ravi, do you have the approximate request rate in that bad window? Like RPS.

[03:19] Ravi Iyer: I can share ranges. We don’t want exact numbers in a recording, sorry. But it’s within what we said: peak-like, call it “tens to low hundreds per second” range.

[03:30] Soojin Lee: That’s totally fine. Also for public write-up we can avoid exact traffic volumes and use relative throughput ranges.

[03:36] Maya Chen: Yeah, we can’t publish volumes. Competitors would love that.

[03:40] Markus Klein: Understood. If you can send the run config out-of-band, that’s enough for me.

[03:47] Sana Farid: One more: what was the prompt and output lengths? Roughly.

[03:52] Ravi Iyer: Prompts are around 1–2k tokens. Output is usually structured JSON under 300 tokens, but occasionally it goes longer when the model gets chatty.

[04:03] Markus Klein: Okay. So if it “gets chatty,” that can dominate total latency. Do you enforce a max tokens cap?

[04:09] Ravi Iyer: We do, but our cap is… generous. We can tighten it for the benchmark if needed.

[04:16] Maya Chen: We can’t tighten too much in prod because then we get malformed outputs.

[04:20] Markus Klein: Right, right. Another thing: did you see more retries or 429s yesterday?

[04:26] Ravi Iyer: Actually yes. Not a ton, but more 429 than Tuesday.

[04:31] Markus Klein: That’s a signal. If your client retries, you can get bursty load and queueing.

[04:37] Priyom Das: And we had talked about setting the quota high enough so you wouldn’t hit that. Maybe we’re still throttling at the gateway.

[04:44] Sana Farid: Or the retry policy is too aggressive. Like immediate retry causing thundering herd.

[04:50] Ravi Iyer: We use exponential backoff but it starts at 200ms.

[04:53] Markus Klein: That’s pretty tight. (laughs) For inference, 200ms means “I’m about to punch you again.”

[05:00] Elena Park: Okay but we can adjust. We were just trying to keep P95 down.

[05:04] Markus Klein: Yep, understood.

[05:06] Priyom Das: So, on next steps: Markus can pull traces from our side. We can correlate queue time vs compute time. I’ll also check the throttling settings.

[05:16] Markus Klein: Yeah, I’ll grab the Console trace view for that window. If it’s queueing, we’ll see “pre-fill wait” or “scheduler wait.”

[05:26] Ravi Iyer: Great.

[05:27] Sana Farid: And can you send us the client-side histogram? Even a screenshot. If TTFT is stable but total moves, that points to decode length or decode scheduling.

[05:36] Ravi Iyer: Yep.

[05:38] Priyom Das: Before we get too deep: are we still on track for the POC timeline? You had said two more weeks for decision.

[05:45] Elena Park: Yes, but the p95 has to be stable. Procurement won’t start until we have a stable story.

[05:52] Priyom Das: Got it.

[05:54] Soojin Lee: Elena, can I ask one question on the case study side, just to set up? Assuming we fix p95, are you aiming for a public case study with name/logo, or something more limited?

[06:05] Elena Park: Public with logo is possible, but we’ll need review. Dinesh will gate the security language. Also we may need to exclude specific regions and internal project names.

[06:16] Dinesh Patel: And no architecture diagram that shows network topology. High-level is fine.

[06:22] Soojin Lee: Yep. High-level block diagram is usually enough: “QuantaPay app → Redwood endpoint → post-processing,” no subnets.

[06:30] Maya Chen: We can do that. We like the marketing angle if it’s about “latency and reliability” rather than “we are using model X for fraud.”

[06:40] Priyom Das: Makes sense.

[06:41] Markus Klein: Let’s go back to the numbers for a sec, because wording depends on what’s true. Ravi, Tuesday’s run: what did you see for p50 and p95 relative improvement?

[06:52] Ravi Iyer: Roughly, p50 improved like 30-ish percent compared to our vLLM setup. p95 was similar improvement, maybe 20%. But then the bad window, p95 was worse than baseline.

[07:06] Markus Klein: That’s helpful. And baseline is your current self-hosted vLLM on A10s?

[07:12] Ravi Iyer: Close. Different GPU, but yes self-hosted.

[07:16] Markus Klein: Okay.

[07:18] Sana Farid: For publication, we’d need the baseline environment described in a way that’s accurate but not too specific. Like “previous self-managed inference stack” is safe. But if we want to claim % improvement, we should note it’s from a “production-like replay” and include the query shape. Otherwise people think it’s universal.

[07:36] Soojin Lee: Exactly. We can say “In a controlled traffic replay representing QuantaPay’s peak query mix…” and then list ranges: prompt tokens ~1–2k, output tokens <300, JSON structure.

[07:49] Maya Chen: As long as we don’t say “peak volume is X.”

[07:51] Soojin Lee: We won’t.

[07:53] Priyom Das: Also, we need to be careful: we can’t say “guaranteed” unless it’s in the SLA.

[07:59] Soojin Lee: Yep. We say “observed” results during the measurement window.

[08:05] Markus Klein: Good guardrails.

[08:07] Elena Park: I do want a concrete statement, though. Not just “it’s better.”

[08:12] Soojin Lee: Totally. Concrete but scoped.

[08:15] Sana Farid: What I typically do is propose 2–3 candidate claim sentences, then legal/security picks. Like:
- “Reduced p95 latency by X% at comparable throughput in a production-like traffic replay.”
- “Lowered cost per 1K tokens by Y% after enabling batching and cache policies.”
But we need validated windows and sources.

[08:35] Ravi Iyer: On cost, we haven’t finished. But it seems lower than Bedrock for sure. Like, materially.

[08:43] Priyom Das: You said Bedrock on the call last week. If you want, we can keep competitor names out of the case study and just talk about “managed API baseline.”

[08:52] Maya Chen: Please do. We don’t want to poke AWS.

[08:55] Markus Klein: (laughs) fair.

[08:56] Elena Park: Internally, it’s Bedrock and some Together tests. Externally, “prior approach.”

[09:03] Soojin Lee: Exactly.

[09:05] Markus Klein: On the regression: do you remember if that coincided with you enabling the fallback policy?

[09:11] Ravi Iyer: We did toggle fallback from “off” to “on.” But it wasn’t failing over, I think.

[09:17] Markus Klein: Even with fallback enabled, there’s minimal overhead. But if it was actually failing over to a different variant, you’d see a tail bump.

[09:25] Ravi Iyer: We didn’t see a different model in the logs.

[09:28] Sana Farid: Could it be cold starts? Like the pool autoscaled?

[09:32] Markus Klein: Dedicated pool doesn’t cold start in the same way, but if we scaled up worker count, the cache warmup can matter.

[09:41] Elena Park: We did ask for burst behavior. Could that have triggered something?

[09:45] Markus Klein: It can. If we allow bursting, the scheduler behavior changes. Again, trace will tell us.

[09:52] Priyom Das: There’s also a support ticket we opened yesterday — I think SUP-2444 — about latency regression in that window. That’s tracking it.

[10:01] Ravi Iyer: Great, yes. That’s the one.

[10:03] Markus Klein: So this is not “hand-wavy.” We’ll treat it like an incident investigation.

[10:09] Dinesh Patel: For public case study, please don’t mention “incident” or “regression” obviously.

[10:13] Soojin Lee: Yeah, public story would only include stabilized outcomes and maybe a generic line like “worked closely during onboarding to tune batching” — no negatives.

[10:23] Maya Chen: Thank you.

[10:25] Priyom Das: Okay. Let’s talk about the “measurable outcomes” piece. Elena, what would you want to be able to say publicly if we nail this?

[10:34] Elena Park: Two things: 1) latency and predictability; 2) operationally less headache than maintaining our own stack.

[10:43] Markus Klein: That second one is big. People underestimate on-call.

[10:46] Elena Park: Exactly. But it’s hard to quantify.

[10:49] Sana Farid: Sometimes you can quantify “engineering hours saved” or “reduced paging” but it gets squishy. If you can say “cut weekly maintenance from X hours to Y” that’s measurable.

[11:00] Elena Park: Maybe. We’d need to sanity check with my team.

[11:03] Soojin Lee: If it’s not measurable, we can frame as a quote rather than a headline metric. Like a direct Elena quote: “We no longer have to babysit GPU capacity and kernel upgrades.”

[11:15] Maya Chen: That’s acceptable.

[11:18] Ravi Iyer: On latency, I’m comfortable with % changes, but I want it to be honest. The improvements depend on prompt sizes and concurrency.

[11:26] Sana Farid: 100%. That’s why we’ll include the ranges and window.

[11:31] Markus Klein: And we can also pick the metric that is most stable. Sometimes TTFT is very stable and total is sensitive to output length. If your user experience cares about total, we should publish total, but we might also mention TTFT for streaming UX.

[11:46] Maya Chen: Our UI shows streaming, but we still parse the final JSON. So TTFT is a “nice to have,” total is the KPI.

[11:54] Markus Klein: Got it.

[11:55] Priyom Das: Another question: can we publish deployment mode? Like “Dedicated capacity.”

[12:01] Elena Park: Yes, that’s fine.

[12:03] Dinesh Patel: Just don’t publish the cloud region or the exact isolation model.

[12:07] Priyom Das: Understood.

[12:08] Soojin Lee: Great. “Dedicated capacity with isolation controls” is usually safe.

[12:13] Markus Klein: Going back to the 429s: are those from us, or from your own gateway?

[12:18] Ravi Iyer: From you, I think. Response includes a header indicating rate limit.

[12:23] Markus Klein: Okay. Then we need to raise the POC quota or tune the retry behavior. For benchmark, you don’t want throttling to distort p95.

[12:35] Sana Farid: Exactly. If 1% of requests get throttled and retried, p95 can move a lot.

[12:42] Ravi Iyer: That might be it. Because our retry makes total look bad.

[12:46] Markus Klein: Yep.

[12:48] Priyom Das: I’ll take that as an action item — adjust quota on the Dedicated endpoint. Markus, can you help me with what to change?

[12:55] Markus Klein: Yep.

[12:57] Elena Park: One more thing: we noticed output format drift a bit when we pushed concurrency. Like occasional malformed JSON.

[13:05] Markus Klein: Is that with structured output turned on? Or just prompting?

[13:08] Ravi Iyer: Prompting. We didn’t enable structured output mode yet.

[13:12] Markus Klein: Okay. Structured output can help, but it can add a tiny bit of overhead. We can test it. For case study, that’s a nice “quality + reliability” angle if it actually improves parse success.

[13:26] Soojin Lee: But again, only if we can measure it. Like “reduced invalid JSON responses from A% to B%.”

[13:33] Maya Chen: That would be huge for us.

[13:35] Elena Park: But we need to validate that it doesn’t increase latency.

[13:38] Markus Klein: Exactly. We can A/B within the replay harness.

[13:44] Priyom Das: Would you rather keep focus on latency first, then quality?

[13:48] Elena Park: Yes. Fix p95, then we can talk quality.

[13:52] Markus Klein: Great.

[13:54] Sana Farid: For the metrics worksheet: I’ll propose we track four core measures:
1) p50 / p95 total latency
2) error rate (including 429s and parse failures)
3) throughput at steady-state concurrency
4) cost per request or per 1K tokens
And for each, we define the window and data source.

[14:14] Ravi Iyer: That’s good. We can provide our baseline for 1 and 2.

[14:18] Sana Farid: Perfect.

[14:20] Soojin Lee: And then for case study copy we’ll pick one headline metric (usually p95 + cost) and make the rest “supporting proof points.”

[14:29] Elena Park: I like that.

[14:31] Markus Klein: Alright. Can we talk about the dedicated pool sizing? I want to make sure we’re not accidentally under-provisioned for your spike profile.

[14:39] Ravi Iyer: Current pool size is what you recommended. It worked Tuesday.

[14:44] Markus Klein: So probably not capacity. But I want to see GPU utilization. If you’re at 95% constantly, tail latency worsens.

[14:52] Ravi Iyer: We can look.

[14:54] Markus Klein: I’ll pull GPU util graphs too.

[14:57] Priyom Das: Quick check: we’re still aligned that if we hit targets, QuantaPay is open to being a reference call and a public case study, right?

[15:05] Elena Park: Yes, with the caveats. And we may limit reference calls frequency.

[15:10] Priyom Das: Totally. We can do, like, one per quarter, prepped.

[15:14] Dinesh Patel: And no calls with competitors.

[15:16] Priyom Das: (laughs) we can’t always control who’s on the prospect side, but we can screen. We do qualified prospects only.

[15:23] Soojin Lee: We also do a pre-brief and a do-not-discuss list. That’s standard.

[15:28] Elena Park: Okay.

[15:30] Markus Klein: Back to technical: do you have any logs showing server-side timeouts?

[15:35] Ravi Iyer: No server logs, just client.

[15:38] Markus Klein: Okay. If we see timeouts, we’ll share request IDs and you can correlate.

[15:44] Sana Farid: Also, for the case study, we should avoid claiming “always” or “guaranteed.” We can say “met SLO in the measured window.”

[15:54] Maya Chen: Yes, please.

[15:56] Priyom Das: Soojin, any specific phrasing recommendations?

[16:00] Soojin Lee: Two patterns that tend to survive legal review:
- “In a production-like benchmark, QuantaPay observed up to X% improvement in p95 latency after moving to Redwood Dedicated.”
- “After tuning batching and rate limits, QuantaPay achieved [range] p95 latency while sustaining [range] throughput.”
We can replace numbers later.

[16:22] Elena Park: “Up to” is okay, but we don’t want it to sound like marketing fluff.

[16:26] Soojin Lee: Totally fair. Another option is: “Observed X% improvement” without “up to,” but then we must pick the exact window and keep it consistent.

[16:36] Sana Farid: That’s why we need a measurement window definition. Like: “7-day average during June 10–17” or “three replay runs with same config.”

[16:46] Ravi Iyer: I’d prefer something like “median of three runs.”

[16:49] Sana Farid: That’s actually very strong statistically. We can do that.

[16:54] Markus Klein: Great.

[16:55] Priyom Das: Okay. Let’s lock the plan.

[17:00] Markus Klein: Before we close: any other issues? Anything with the SDK integration?

[17:05] Ravi Iyer: SDK is fine. We did have one weird thing where function calling was… I think your docs call it tool calling? It returned a different schema.

[17:13] Markus Klein: Yeah, docs say tool calling. That might be a model-specific behavior. For POC, are you using tool calling or just structured JSON?

[17:22] Ravi Iyer: Just structured JSON via prompt.

[17:25] Markus Klein: Then ignore tool calling for now.

[17:28] Maya Chen: One more question: can we do an architecture diagram for the case study? Like, simple.

[17:35] Soojin Lee: Yes, but we’ll keep it at the “component” level. No VPC diagram. Also we can run it by Dinesh early.

[17:44] Dinesh Patel: Please do.

[17:46] Priyom Das: Alright.

[17:48] Markus Klein: I’ll recap technical next steps:
1) I pull traces for the bad window and see if queueing/429s are the culprit.
2) Priyom adjusts quota, maybe we reduce throttling.
3) You send replay config + client histograms.
4) We rerun with controlled settings, possibly cap batching, and compare.

[18:08] Elena Park: Sounds right.

[18:10] Sana Farid: And I’ll draft the metrics table + claim wording options.

[18:14] Soojin Lee: And I’ll help translate that into a case-study-safe narrative.

[18:18] Priyom Das: Great. Can we tentatively schedule the technical deep dive for Tuesday?

[18:23] Ravi Iyer: Tuesday morning works.

[18:25] Elena Park: Yeah.

[18:26] Priyom Das: I’ll send options.

[18:28] Markus Klein: Last thing — if the p95 regression is due to a model build change, we can pin to the older build while we fix. That’s doable.

[18:37] Elena Park: Good to know.

[18:40] Priyom Das: Okay, thanks everyone. We’ll follow up in email with action items and next meeting.

[18:46] Maya Chen: Thanks.

[18:47] Dinesh Patel: Thanks.

[18:48] Ravi Iyer: Thanks.

[18:49] Elena Park: Bye.

---

Auto-generated Notes (Fireflies)
Action items:
- Redwood to investigate p95 regression window using traces and quota/rate limit settings.
- QuantaPay to share replay config + baseline metrics screenshots.
- Redwood to draft publishable metrics wording with caveats for case study.

Questions captured:
- Can we publish throughput/traffic volume? (Answer: only ranges, no exact volumes.)
- Can we publish architecture? (Answer: high-level only; no network topology.)
